newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat suspect to appear before Zagreb judges.
newsitem.headline: Croat suspect to appear before Zagreb judges.

text.p: Indicted Bosnian Croat war crimes suspect Pero Skopljak, arrested by Croatian authorities last week and held in a Zagreb jail, will not leave Croatia for a couple of weeks, his lawyer said on Tuesday.

Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac said Skopljak would appear before a panel of county court judges who would not decide about his possible extradition to The Hague war crimes tribunal before the end of next week.
Skopljak, accused of persecuting Bosnian Moslems during the 1993-94 Moslem-Croat war, would then have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court.
"There is a procedure prescribed by law in such cases and it has to be observed," Slokovic-Glumac told Reuters.
The Croatian Justice Ministry released a statement late on Monday signed by Justice Minister Miroslav Separovic, giving the first official confirmation Skopljak had been apprehended.
Slokovic-Glumac said Skopljak was being held at Remetinec county jail in a Zagreb suburb after being arrested by civilian police at the house he lived in, in Samobor near Zagreb.

Skopljak was indicted by the tribunal in November 1995 for persecuting Bosnian Moslems on political, racial and religious grounds between May 1992 and May 1993. He had been chief of police in the central Bosnian town of Vitez during that time.

He was indicted along with Dario Kordic, the most wanted Bosnian Croat war crimes suspect, and four others. They are alleged to have imprisoned Moslem civilians, tortured them, used them as human shields and forced labour and murdered or otherwise killed some of the detainees.
Skopljak's lawyer said his client, if extradited to The Hague and tried, would plead not guilty.

"We completely negate all the charges made by the prosecution. (My client) did not hold any political, military or police position at the time when the deeds he was incriminated with allegedly took place," Slokovic-Glumac said. "Specifically, he was not the chief of Vitez police at the time of the Moslem-Croat war. He stepped down in 1991," she added.

Skopljak's detention comes amid intense international pressure on the former warring factions in ex-Yugoslavia to turn over war crimes suspects to the Hague tribunal -- the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held after World War Two.
Foreign envoys have repeatedly told Croatian President Franjo Tudjman that they expect him to use his influence over Bosnian Croats to get them to hand over indictees.
